statement.text:
Thermoelectric effects and their applications in thermoelectric generator and refrigerator (10 pt)


Introduction: Thermoelectric effects


Thermoelectric effects in conducting materials are due to the interplay between heat current and electrical current. In this problem we consider only three predominant thermoelectric effects, namely the Joule, the Seebeck and the Peltier effects, neglecting the others.


The Joule effect
 is a consequence of the interaction between electrical carriers and crystal lattice. Moving directionally in presence of electrical current, carriers transfer a part of their energy to the vibrating crystal lattice, and as a result the crystal is heated. The Joule effect is irreversible.


The Seebeck effect
 can be observed in a thermocouple consisting of two dissimilar conducting bars A and B connecting by direct junction (Fig. 1a) or junction via an intermediate material C (Fig. 1b). The material C is good electrical conductor with very small specific heat. When the two junctions of the thermocouple are maintained at different temperatures 
\(T_1\)
 and 
\(T_2\)
 (Fig. 1a,b) the Seebeck electromotive force (
emf
) is produced 
\[\begin{equation}
\epsilon = \alpha(T_1 - T_2) \tag{1}
\end{equation}\]
 where 
\(\alpha\)
 is the Seebeck coefficient of the thermocouple. 
\(\alpha\)
 is considered temperature independent .


The Seebeck effect is applied in thermoelectric generator to convert heat energy into electrical one.











Figure 1. (a) direct junctions. (b) junctions via an intermediate material C. (1) Heat source (temperature 
\(T_1\)
); (2) Heat sink (temperature 
\(T_2\)
)




The Peltier effect


Whenever current passes through a thermocouple circuit consisted of two dissimilar conductors A and B with direct junctions (Fig. 2a) or junctioned via intermediate conductor C (Fig. 2b), depending on the current direction, heat is either absorbed or released at the junctions of the two conductors. This is the Peltier effect. The Peltier heat power 
q
 appeared at a junction is 
\[\begin{equation}
q = \pi I \tag{2}
\end{equation}\]
 
\(\pi\)
 is the Peltier coefficient of this junction.The Seebeck and Peltier effects are reversible effects in contrast to the irreversible Joule effect. Although the Seebeck and Peltier effects need junctions between the thermoelements, they are essentially bulk effects. A closed electrical cycle in a thermocouple with the Peltier effect (Fig. 2b) can be used as a refrigerator when heat is removed from one isolated junction and rejected at the other.


For simplicity, the heat radiation, circulation, conduction through surrounding environment are considered negligible, and heat current is supposed to be inside the thermocouple and at the heat source and the heat sink.

solution.text:
Theory Q3


Thermoelectric effects and theirapplication in thermoelectric generator and refrigerator(10 points)


Solution and Marking scheme




A. Heat transfer and thermoelectric generator


A1. Heat transfer in a homogeneous conducting bar





A1.10.75 pt


Consider heat transfer in the segment 
\(dx\)
 of the bar in the steady state. Equation for the balance of the energy exchange through the cross-sectional area is written as 
\[-kS\frac{dT\left(x\right)}{dx} + \rho\frac{dx}{S}I^2 = -kS\frac{dT\left(x + dx\right)}{dx} = -kS\frac{dT\left(x\right)}{dx} - kS\frac{d^2T\left(x\right)}{dx^2}.dx\]
 Hence 
\[-kS\frac{d^2T\left(x\right)}{dx^2} = \frac{\rho I^2}{S} \tag*{(A1)\qquad\textbf{0.25}}\]
 Integration of (A1) gives 
\[\frac{dT\left(x\right)}{dx} = -\frac{\rho I^2}{kS^2}x + C_1, \tag*{(A2)}\]
 
\[T\left(x\right) = -\frac{\rho I^2}{2kS^2}x^2 + C_1x + C_2. \tag*{(A3)}\]
 Constants 
\(C_1\)
, 
\(C_2\)
 are derived from the boundary conditions 
\[x = 0 \Rightarrow T = T_1 \Rightarrow C_2 = T_1, \tag*{(A4)\qquad\textbf{0.25}}\]
 
\[x = L \Rightarrow T = T_2 \Rightarrow C_1 = \frac{T_2 - T_1}{L} + \frac{1}{2}\frac{\rho L}{S^2k}I^2. \tag*{(A5)}\]
 Equation for the temperature distribution in the bar is 
\[T\left(x\right) = T_1 + \left(\frac{\rho LI^2}{2kS^2} - \frac{T_1 - T_2}{L}\right)x - \frac{\rho I^2}{2kS^2}x^2. \tag*{(A6)\qquad\textbf{0.25}}\]





A1.21.0 pt


Using (A2) –(A5) we obtain the equation for the heat current at 
\(x\)
 
\[q\left(x\right) = -kS\frac{dT\left(x\right)}{dx} = \frac{kS}{L}(T_1 - T_2) + \frac{\rho I^2}{S}\left(x - \frac{L}{2}\right), \tag*{(A7)\qquad\textbf{0.5}}\]
 at 
\(x = 0\)
, and 
\(x = L\)
 
\[q\left(x = 0\right) = \frac{kS}{L}\left(T_1 - T_2\right) - \frac{\rho LI^2}{2S} = K\left(T_1 - T_2\right) - \frac{RI^2}{2}, \tag*{(A8)\qquad\textbf{0.25}}\]
 
\[q\left(x = L\right) = \frac{kS}{L}\left(T_1 - T_2\right) + \frac{\rho LI^2}{2S} = K\left(T_1 - T_2\right) + \frac{RI^2}{2}. \tag*{(A9)\qquad\textbf{0.25}}\]
 Here 
\(K = \dfrac{kS}{L}\)
, 
\(R = \dfrac{\rho L}{S}\)
.





A2. Relation between Peltier and Seebeck Coefficients


Thermocouple consists of two subsystems: a) the conducting electron gas that performs an ideal themodynamic cycle; b) Nuclei and bounded electrons of the bar crystal that oscillate around equillibrium positions at finite temperature and participate in heat conduction process. If the resistance of the thermocouple is neglected, these two subsystems may be considered as noninteracting, the electron gas exchanges heat only with the heat source at 
\(T_{\mathit{1}}\)
 and the heat sink at 
\(T_{\mathit{2}\,,}\)
 performing the ideal Carnot cycle.





A2.10.25 pt


Electron gas receives heat from heat source due to the Peltier effect
0.25
 
\[q_1 = \pi_1I \tag*{(A10)}\]





A2.2.0.25 pt


The heat amount transferred to the heat sink due to the Peltier effect
0.25
 
\[q_2 = \pi_2I \tag*{(A11)}\]





A2.3.0.5 pt


Power delivered by the electron gas due to the Seebeck emf is
0.5
 
\[P = \varepsilon I = \alpha\left(T_1 - T_2\right)I \tag*{(A12)}\]





A2.40.5 pt


The efficiency of the ideal Carnot cycle applied to the thermocouple can be written as 
\[\eta = \frac{P}{q_1}, \eta = \frac{T_1 - T_2}{T_1}. \tag*{(A13)\qquad\textbf{0.25}}\]
 Thus 
\[\frac{T_1 - T_2}{T_1} = \frac{\alpha\left(T_1 - T_2\right)}{\pi_1} \tag*{(A14)}\]
 Comparing these equations, one has 
\(\pi_1 = \alpha T_1\)
 .
0.25


This is the Peltier coefficient at the first junction contacting with the heat source.


Generally, one has 
\(\pi = \alpha T\)
.





A3. Thermoelectric generator





A.3.1.0.5 pt


Power received by the thermocouple from the heat source (see also (A8)) is 
\[q_1 = K\left(T_1 - T_2\right) + \alpha T_1I - \frac{1}{2}I^2R. \tag*{(A15)\qquad\textbf{0.25}}\]
 Here
\(\,\alpha\)
 is the Seebeck coefficient of the thermocouple and 
\[K = K_A + K_B = \frac{k_AS_A}{L} + \frac{k_BS_B}{L}, \tag*{(A16)}\]
 
\[R = R_A + R_B = \frac{\rho_AL}{S_A} + \frac{\rho_BL}{S_B}, \tag*{(A17)}\]
 are its thermal conductance and internal resistance.


The heat sink receives a power (see also (A9)) 
\[q_2 = K\left(T_1 - T_2\right) + \alpha T_2I + \frac{1}{2}I^2R. \tag*{(A.18)\qquad\textbf{0.25}}\]





A3.2.0.75 pt


The efficiency of the thermoelectric generator is 
\[\eta = \frac{P_L}{q_1} = \frac{I^2R_L}{K\left(T_1 - T_2\right) + \alpha T_1I - I^2R/2} = \frac{m}{\dfrac{K\left(T_1 - T_2\right)}{I^2R} + \dfrac{\alpha T_1}{IR} - \dfrac{1}{2}}. \tag*{(A19)\qquad\textbf{0.25}}\]
 Here we use 
\(R_L = mR\)
. The electrical current in the circuit is 
\[I = \frac{\alpha\left(T_1 - T_2\right)}{R_L + R} = \frac{\alpha\left(T_1 - T_2\right)}{\left(1 + m\right)R}. \tag*{(A20)\qquad\textbf{0.25}}\]
 Substituting (A20) into (A19) we obtain the expession for the efficiency 
\[\eta = \frac{m\left(T_1 - T_2\right)}{\dfrac{KR\left(1 + m\right)^2}{\alpha^2} + T_1\left(1 + m\right) - \dfrac{T_1 - T_2}{2}}. \tag*{(A21)\qquad\textbf{0.25}}\]





A3.3.0.25


Replacing the figure of merit 
\[Z = \frac{\alpha^2}{KR} \tag*{(A22)}\]
 and 
\(\eta_c = \dfrac{T_1 - T_2}{T_1}\)
 the efficiency of the ideal Carnot cycle in (A21), one has 
\[\eta = \eta_c\frac{m}{\dfrac{\left(1 + m\right)^2}{ZT_1} + \left(1 + m\right) - \dfrac{1}{2}\eta_c}. \tag*{(A23)\qquad\textbf{0.25}}\]
 From (A23) one sees that  larger 
\(Z\)
 leads to the larger efficiency of the corresponding thermoelectric generator. The condition 
\(ZT_1 \geq 1\)
 can be used for material application in thermoelectric generators.





A4. The maximum efficiency





A4.10.25 pt


When
\(\,R_L = R\)
 or 
m=1,
 the power consumed on the load is maximum. The efficiency in that case is 
\[\eta_P = \frac{T_1 - T_1}{\left[\dfrac{4}{Z} + \dfrac{3T_1 + T_2}{2}\right]}. \tag*{(A24)\qquad\textbf{0.25}}\]





A4.2.0.75 pt


Equation (A23) may be rewritten as 
\[\eta = \frac{m}{a\left(1 + m\right)^2 + b\left(1 + m\right) - 1/2}, \tag*{(A25)\qquad\textbf{0.25}}\]
 where 
\(a = \dfrac{1}{Z\left(T_1 - T_2\right)}\)
 , 
\(b = \dfrac{T_1}{T_1 - T_2}\)
 .


Equation 
\(\dfrac{d\eta}{dm} = 0\)

\(M = \sqrt{1 + \dfrac{2b - 1}{2a}}\)
 or
0.25
 
\[M = \sqrt{1 + Z\frac{\left(T_1 + T_2\right)}{2}}. \tag*{(A26)\qquad\textbf{0.25}}\]





A4.3.0.25 pt


Using (A25), (A26) we obtain the maximum efficiency of the thermoelectric generator
0.25
 
\[\eta_{\max} = \frac{T_1 - T_2}{T_1}\frac{\left(M - 1\right)}{\left(M + \dfrac{T_2}{T_1}\right)} \tag*{(A27)}\]

B. Thermoelectric refrigerator


B1. The cooling power and the maximum temperature difference





B1.10.25pt


For cooling purpose we choose the current direction so that heat is absorbed at upper junction (temperature 
\(T_{\mathit{1}}\)
) due to Peltier effect and transferred to the A & B bars. Using (A.9) one gets cooling power taken out from heat source at 
\(T_{\mathit{1}}\)
0.25
 
\[q_C = \alpha T_1I + K\left(T_1 - T_2\right) - \frac{RI^2}{2} \tag*{(B.1)}\]
 where
\(\,K, R\)
 are thermal conductance and internal resistance of thermocouple.





B1.2.0.5


Condition for the maximum cooling power
\(\,q_{CM}\)

\(\dfrac{dq_C}{dI} = 0\)
, one has
0.25
 
\[I_q = \frac{\alpha T_1}{R}, \tag*{(B2)}\]
 
\[q_{CM} = \frac{\alpha^2T_1}{2R} - K\left(T_2 - T_1\right). \tag*{(B3)}\]
 .


The maximum temperature depression is derived from the condition 
\(q_{CM} = 0\)
, which gives 
\[\Delta T_{\max} = T_2 - T_{1\mathrm{min}} = \frac{\alpha^2T_{1\mathrm{min}}^2}{2KR} = \frac{ZT_{1\mathrm{min}}^2}{2}. \tag*{(B4)\qquad\textbf{0.25}}\]
 Here 
\(Z = \dfrac{\alpha^2}{KR}\)
 is the figure of merit of the thermocouple.

B2.10.25pt

\[0 = T_{1\mathrm{min}}^2 + \frac{2}{Z_m}T_{1\mathrm{min}} - \frac{2}{Z_m}T_2\]
 
\[T_{1\mathrm{min}} = \frac{1}{Z_m}\left(\sqrt{1 + 2Z_mT_2} - 1\right). \tag*{(B5)\qquad\textbf{0.1}}\]
 Putting
\(\,T_2 = 300\mathrm{K}\)
 and  
\(Z_m = 3.15\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{K}^{-1}\)
in (B.5) we obtain 
\[T_{1\mathrm{min}} = 2.22\times10^2\,\mathrm{K}. \tag*{(B.6)\qquad\textbf{0.15}}\]





B2.2.0.5


Putting the value of the internal resistance

0.25


in (B2), one gets the working current 
\[I_\mathrm{W} = \frac{\alpha T_{1\mathrm{min}}}{R} = \frac{4.2\times10^{-4}\times221.5}{4\times10^{-3}}\mathrm{A} = 23.3\mathrm{A} \tag*{(B7)\qquad\textbf{0.25}}\]





B3. The coefficient of performance





B3.10.5pt


According to the energy conservation law, the power supplied by the electrical source 
\(P\)
 equals to the Joule heat plus Peltier’s heat taken away in thermocouple per unit of time: 
\[P = \alpha(T_2 - T_1)I + RI^2\ \ . \tag*{(B.8)\qquad\textbf{0.25}}\]
 The equation for Coefficient of Performance (COP) is 
\[\beta = \frac{q_C}{P} = \frac{\alpha T_1I - K\left(T_2 - T_1\right) - \dfrac{RI^2}{2}}{\alpha(T_2 - T_1)I + RI^2} \tag*{(B9)\qquad\textbf{0.25}}\]





B3.2.0.25


Electrical current 
\(I_\beta\)
 corresponds to the maximum of the COP is found from the equation
\(\,\dfrac{d\beta}{dI} = 0\)
. (B9) may be rewritten in convenience form 
\[\beta = -\frac{1}{2} + \frac{\alpha\left(T_1 + T_2\right)I - 2K\left(T_2 - T_1\right)}{2\left[\alpha(T_2 - T_1) + RI\right]I}\quad. \tag*{(B10)}\]
 The equation 
\(\dfrac{d\beta}{dI} = 0\)
 leads to 
\[-\alpha R\left(T_1 + T_2\right)I^2 + 4K\left(T_2 - T_1\right)RI + 2K\alpha\left(T_2 - T_1\right)^2 = 0,\]
 
\[I^2 - \frac{2K\left(T_2 - T_1\right)I}{\alpha T_M} - \frac{K}{RT_M}\left(T_2 - T_1\right)^2 = 0, \tag*{(B.11)}\]
 with  
\(\mathrm{T}_M = \dfrac{\left(T_2 + T_1\right)}{2}\)
.(B.12)


Solution of (B.11) is 
\[I_\beta = \frac{K\left(T_2 - T_1\right)}{\alpha T_M}\left\{\sqrt{1 + Z\,\mathrm{T}_M} + 1\right\}. \tag*{(B.13)\qquad\textbf{0.25}}\]
 (
Taking into account that
 
\(Z = \dfrac{\alpha^2}{KR}\)
, (B.13) can be written in other form
 
\[I_\beta = \frac{\alpha\left(T_2 - T_1\right)}{R\left\{\sqrt{1 + Z\,\mathrm{T}_M} - 1\right\}}\mathit{)} \tag*{(B.14)}\]





B3.3.0.25


Substituting (B.14) into (B.9) one has
0.25
 
\[\beta_{\max} = \frac{T_1\left[\sqrt{1 + ZT_M} - T_2/T_1\right]}{\left(T_2 - T_1\right)\left[\sqrt{1 + ZT_M} + 1\right]}. \tag*{(B.15)}\]
